pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 7–9 — the ocean has tides (water rises/falls ~twice a day, mainly from the Moon's gravity), waves (made by wind blowing across the surface), and currents (large flows that carry heat and nutrients around the globe).
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 geography (physical processes; coasts) and science forces (Y5 gravity, Y3 forces) — the Moon's gravitational pull and wind as a force are the mechanisms.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 5-PS2-1 (gravity's pull) and ESS2 Earth systems (interactions of the geosphere/hydrosphere/atmosphere) — distinct causes for three distinct phenomena.
• Operational details: the crux is matching THREE phenomena to THREE distinct causes and NOT conflating them: tides = Moon's gravity (regular daily rise/fall), waves = wind (energy moves through water, water doesn't travel far), currents = large-scale flows (driven by wind + temperature/density) carrying heat and nutrients. The subtle wave idea — energy travels, the water mostly stays put and bobs — is a classic error worth targeting. Keep tide mechanism at 'the Moon pulls the water' (bulge model); full two-bulge/Sun detail is later.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7–8): matches each phenomenon to the right cause (Moon/wind/flow); Tier B (~8–9): describes tides as regular Moon-driven rise/fall and waves as wind-made; Tier C (~9): explains a current carries heat/nutrients around the world, and that a wave moves energy while the water largely stays in place.
bestPractices: Teach the three as THREE separate cause–effect stories so they aren't blurred: Moon→tides, wind→waves, big flows→currents.
Target the wave misconception directly with a bob-in-place demonstration (a float rises and falls but doesn't travel with the wave) — energy moves, water mostly stays.
Model tides with a simple Moon-pulls-a-bulge representation and connect to the regular, predictable twice-daily rhythm children can relate to coastal timing.
Show currents as global conveyor paths carrying WARMTH and NUTRIENTS — tie to why some coasts are milder and why nutrient-rich currents teem with life (links to food webs/climate).
Use predict-then-check manipulation (change the wind, move the Moon) so causes are felt, not just told.
keyRepresentations: A Moon–Earth–water bulge diagram showing the tide following the Moon
A wave cross-section with a bobbing float showing energy travelling while water stays put
A world map of major surface currents with warm/cold colouring and nutrient flow
Three cause–effect cards: Moon→tide, wind→wave, flow→current
commonMisconceptions: Conflating the three — e.g. thinking tides and waves are the same thing, or that waves are caused by the Moon.
'A wave carries the water forward across the sea' — not grasping that the energy travels while the water mostly bobs in place.
'Tides are caused by wind' or 'by the Earth spinning only' — missing the Moon's gravity as the main cause.
'Currents are just where it's windy' — not seeing them as sustained global flows carrying heat and nutrients.
'The Sun has nothing to do with tides' / treating tides as irregular rather than a predictable twice-daily rhythm.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: the ocean moves in three ways, each with its own main cause — tides (the regular, roughly twice-daily rise and fall of the whole sea, caused mainly by the Moon's gravity), waves (quick surface movement made by wind blowing across the water, where energy travels but the water mostly stays put and bobs), and currents (large, steady flows pushed by steady winds and by differences in water temperature and saltiness, which carry warmth and nutrients — and the water itself — around the globe). The central goal is matching each phenomenon to its main cause and NOT conflating them — especially the classic errors 'the wind causes the tide', 'tides and waves are the same', and 'a wave carries the water forward'. Keep the tide mechanism at the simple 'the Moon pulls the water into a bulge' level; the two-bulge model and full Sun detail come later.

activities.title: Three dials for the sea: drive each cause, see a different effect
feedback: If a learner says the wind makes the tide: show the tide still rising on the predictable clock while the wind control is off, and point to the Moon as the driver.
If a learner expects the float to travel with the wave: slow the motion and track the single float rising and falling on the spot — energy passes through, the water bobs.
If a learner blurs wave and current: contrast the float that stays put (wave) with the nutrient particles that drift the whole way across the map (current).
Reinforce correct matches by having them re-state Moon→tide, wind→wave, steady winds and warm/cold, salty water differences→current before moving on.
activities.rationale: Operating each cause separately and seeing a distinct effect recompute is a concrete way to keep the three phenomena from being blurred and to make the energy-vs-water distinction visible rather than merely told. Manipulation is proposed as a strong fit for these cause–effect mechanisms, not as the only way they can be taught.
sourceClaims: Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon (and to a lesser extent the Sun) on Earth's oceans, typically producing two high and two low tides a day.
Ocean surface waves are generated by wind blowing across the water; the wave transmits energy while the water itself mostly moves in place (orbital motion) rather than travelling with the wave.

Ocean currents are large, sustained flows of seawater (driven by wind, temperature and salinity/density differences) that transport heat and nutrients around the globe, influencing climate and marine life.
learnerActions: Spin the Earth under the Moon and watch the ocean bulge stay facing the Moon while a harbour's water rises as it passes under the bulge and falls as it moves away. Real tides keep a predictable clock of about twice a day (roughly every 12½ hours); this simple one-bulge picture shows only one of those high tides.
Turn up a wind control and watch waves grow across the surface while a tethered float lifts and drops in place without travelling along with the wave.
Launch a current across a world map and watch it carry warm/cold colour and drifting nutrient particles across the globe.
After each, state the cause–effect in one sentence: Moon→tide, wind→wave, steady winds and warm/cold, salty water differences→current.
Say in your own words what travels in a wave (energy, while the water mostly stays and bobs) versus what a current carries (heat, nutrients, and even the water itself).
activities.intendedInsight: Tides, waves and currents are three different movements, each with its own main cause (the Moon for tides, wind for waves, steady winds and temperature/saltiness differences for currents); a wave moves energy while the water mostly stays in place, whereas a current actually transports water, heat and nutrients across the planet.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal: three cause–effect stories
feedback: If a card is mismatched, re-show the matching panel and ask which cause belongs with that effect.
Praise a correctly read-back sentence; if the sentence omits the cause, prompt 'and what makes it happen?'.
activities.rationale: Labelled, tappable diagrams present the three cause–effect stories clearly as exposition. This is a presentation/scaffold: it introduces the distinctions but does not let the child vary the cause themselves, so pair it with manipulation or hands-on work to cement the ideas.
sourceClaims: Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon (and to a lesser extent the Sun) on Earth's oceans, typically producing two high and two low tides a day.
Ocean surface waves are generated by wind blowing across the water; the wave transmits energy while the water itself mostly moves in place (orbital motion) rather than travelling with the wave.

Ocean currents are large, sustained flows of seawater (driven by wind, temperature and salinity/density differences) that transport heat and nutrients around the globe, influencing climate and marine life.
learnerActions: Look at three panels — a Moon–Earth–water bulge, a wind-made wave, and a world current map — and tap each cause to reveal 'what makes this happen?'.
On the current map, tap warm and cold flows and name what they carry (heat and nutrients).
Match three cards: Moon→tide, wind→wave, steady winds and warm/cold, salty water differences→current, and read each back as a full sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: Each sea movement has its own clear cause, and the three can be stated as separate cause–effect stories.

activities.title: Blow across a tray of water: predict, observe, explain
feedback: If the child credits their breath with a tide: contrast the calm, windless day where the tide still comes in on schedule with the printable tide table.

If the child says big waves mean high tide: note that waves arrive every few seconds (wind-made) while a tide comes in over roughly six hours (Moon-driven), so wave size and tide state are independent.
Confirm the key separation: tide = slow whole-sea rise/fall from the Moon; wave = quick surface movement from wind; current = ongoing flow driven by wind and by temperature/saltiness.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain task with real water lets the child feel that wind makes waves, then reason that wind cannot explain the regular, clock-like tide — directly confronting the 'wind causes the tide' and 'waves are the tide' misconceptions.
sourceClaims: Ocean surface waves are generated by wind blowing across the water; the wave transmits energy while the water itself mostly moves in place (orbital motion) rather than travelling with the wave.

Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon (and to a lesser extent the Sun) on Earth's oceans, typically producing two high and two low tides a day.
learnerActions: With a shallow tray of water, predict what will happen if you blow gently across the surface, and say why.
Blow and observe the ripples/small waves travelling across.
Explain which of the three movements you just made — a tide, a wave, or a current — and decide whether your breath could have caused a real tide.

Discuss the probes: on a still, windless day would there still be a tide? What in the sky is regular enough to set the tide timetable? If the waves are huge, does that tell you whether it's high or low tide?
activities.intendedInsight: Breath (wind) makes waves, not tides; the tide follows the Moon on a predictable timetable whether it is windy or calm (strong storms can push water a little higher or lower, but they do not make the tide), so wind strength does not tell you the tide state.

activities.title: Beach reasoning: is it the wind, the Moon, or something else?
feedback: If the Sun alone is named as the tide's cause: acknowledge the Sun helps too (about half as much as the Moon), but the Moon is closer and has the bigger effect; link the tide pattern to the Moon's position.
If tide and wave are still merged: use timescales — waves every few seconds from wind, tide over about six hours from the Moon.
For the bottle question, highlight that a current carries the water (and the bottle) along, while a wave passes energy through water that mostly stays put.
activities.rationale: A discriminating scenario that asks both 'is it the wind?' and 'how is a tide different from a wave?' forces the causes apart, since a single 'wind does everything' model cannot answer the second part.
sourceClaims: Ocean currents are large, sustained flows of seawater (driven by wind, temperature and salinity/density differences) that transport heat and nutrients around the globe, influencing climate and marine life.

Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon (and to a lesser extent the Sun) on Earth's oceans, typically producing two high and two low tides a day.
learnerActions: Consider: in the morning the sand is wide and dry; by teatime the sea has crept right up. A child says 'the wind blew the water up the beach.' Decide whether you agree that wind causes the tide.
Explain what actually causes the tide if the wind isn't the reason, and how a tide is different from the waves you jump in.
Answer: could a current carry a message in a bottle across a whole ocean, and how is that different from a wave?
Decide which movement the Sun's gravity also helps cause — the tides — while recognising that the Moon is the closer, dominant cause of the tides.
activities.intendedInsight: A child who assigns the tide to the Moon, waves to the wind, and currents to steady winds and temperature/saltiness differences — and can keep them distinct across new cases — has the concept; attributing the tide to wind is the gap to correct.

constraints: Keep the tide mechanism at the simple 'the Moon pulls the water into a bulge' level for this age; leave the full two-bulge model and detailed Sun contribution for later.

Tap-to-reveal diagrams and matching/recognition checks introduce or verify the distinctions but do not elicit the child independently varying a cause; use them alongside manipulation or hands-on investigation, not as the sole experience.

Matching and multiple-choice checks confirm recognition of cause–effect pairings; they do not by themselves show that the child can construct an explanation, so include tasks that ask for spoken or written reasoning.

A 3D Earth–Moon model could make the tidal geometry slightly more spatial, but 2D representations convey all three phenomena adequately and the wave/current ideas gain little from 3D; treat 3D as optional, not necessary.

The real-water tray and the warm/cold current colouring are approximations: a breath makes only a small ripple, not a true ocean wave, and map colours represent heat transport, not literal water colour.

'Twice a day' and 'about six hours to come in' are age-appropriate idealisations; the single-bulge picture shown in the sim is a simplification and does not itself fully explain the twice-daily rhythm.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the three sources are marked verified:false in the row and were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source framed an in-role chat as unable to carry the key distinctions; this is retained only as a narrow observation that dialogue does not let a child directly manipulate a cause. Dialogue can still support explanation and reasoning, so it is not asserted as a universal law.

The claim that manipulating cause–effect 'directly busts' the wave misconception reflects a catalog preference, not established comparative efficacy; it is presented as a plausible mechanism, not proven superiority over other media.

Tide timing is described as 'about six hours to come in' and 'twice a day' — a child-level approximation (roughly two high and two low tides daily); real tidal periods vary by location and are not exactly 6 hours.

The single-bulge model combined with an orbiting Moon does not on its own produce two high tides per rotation; 'twice a day' is kept as the original's deliberate age simplification with the two-bulge mechanism deferred, and should not be taught as a precise mechanism.

The Sun also contributes indirectly to currents through temperature/density differences; the activity 4 prompt is scoped to the Sun's contribution to tides to keep the intended point clear, not to deny its wider role.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a shallow tray of water and ask them to PREDICT what will happen if they blow gently across the surface, and to say why. They blow and OBSERVE ripples/small waves travelling across. Then ask them to EXPLAIN: which of the three movements did they just make — a tide, a wave, or a current — and could their breath have caused a real tide? The point they must reach is that breath (wind) makes WAVES, not tides; the tide needs the Moon.
probeDeeper: On a completely still, windless day, would there still be a tide? What does that tell you about the cause?
Tides come in and go out on a regular timetable you can print in advance. What in the sky is regular enough to set that timetable?
If I told you the waves were huge today, would that tell you anything about whether it's high or low tide? Why not?
A current can carry a message in a bottle across a whole ocean. How is that different from a wave, which doesn't carry the water along with it?
assess.correctAnswer: The wind does NOT cause the tide. Tides — the slow, twice-a-day rise and fall of the whole sea — are caused mainly by the pull of the Moon's gravity (and a bit the Sun's) on the ocean. Waves are different: those ARE usually made by wind blowing across the water's surface, and they are quick and local. Currents are like rivers of water moving through the ocean, driven by wind at the surface and by differences in temperature and saltiness deeper down. So tide, wave and current are three different movements with three different causes.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The wind causes the tides' — lumps the slow tide together with wind-blown waves under one cause.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a calm windless day (tide still comes in on schedule) with the tide table; introduce the Moon's pull as the clock behind the tide.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the wind blows the sea up the beach, and that's the tide.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the daily rise and fall by wind strength; can't say why tides come at regular clock-like times regardless of how windy it is.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Tides and waves are the same thing' — no distinction between the slow whole-sea rise and the quick surface waves.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Timescales: waves arrive every few seconds and are made by wind; the tide takes about six hours to come in and is made by the Moon.
errorPatterns.distractor: There's no difference — the waves getting bigger IS the tide coming in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses 'tide' and 'wave' interchangeably; says big waves mean high tide.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The Sun causes the tides' or 'the Earth spinning throws the water out' — a cause is offered but the wrong dominant one.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Acknowledge the Sun contributes but the Moon is closer and dominates; link the two-high-tides pattern to the Moon's position.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Sun heats the sea and makes it rise — that's the tide.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the Sun or Earth's spin alone as the tide's cause, leaving the Moon out.

responseLevels.gap: Attributes all sea movement to wind; treats tide, wave and current as the same thing.
responseLevels.full: Cleanly separates the three: tide = slow whole-sea rise/fall driven by the Moon's gravity; waves = quick surface movement made by wind; currents = ongoing flows driven by wind and by temperature/salinity — and uses the causes to reason about new cases (still day still has a tide).
responseLevels.partial: Can name tide, wave and current as different, but muddles their causes — e.g. still credits the tide to wind, or can't say which is Moon-driven and which is wind-driven.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: At the beach in the morning the sand is wide and dry; by teatime the sea has crept right up and covered it. A child says 'that's because the wind blew the water up the beach'. Do you agree that the wind causes the tide — and if the wind isn't the reason, what is, and how is a tide different from the waves you jump in?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who conflates all sea movement with wind will attribute the tide to wind and cannot separate the three; a child with the concept assigns the tide to the Moon, the waves to the wind, and keeps them distinct. Asking both 'is it the wind?' and 'how is a tide different from a wave?' forces the causes apart — a single 'wind does everything' model can't answer the second part.
